Hi everyone,

I’m currently working on an AI-powered fitness automation using n8n, and I would appreciate some guidance from the community on how to design the workflow properly.

The basic idea is to create an automated system where a user first fills out a Google Form with their personal fitness requirements. The form would collect information such as:

  • Name

  • Age

  • Current weight

  • Target weight

  • Fitness goal

    • General fitness

    • Weight loss

    • Weight gain

    • Muscle building

    • Other goals

  • Current fitness level

  • Type of workout they prefer

    • Gym

    • Home workout

    • Outdoor workout

  • Available workout time

  • Dietary preferences

  • Food preferences/restrictions

  • Number of meals they prefer

  • Any relevant limitations or conditions they want the system to consider

Proposed n8n Workflow

I’m thinking of building something like:

Google Form → Google Sheets → n8n → AI → Personalized Fitness Plan → WhatsApp

After the user submits the form, n8n would collect and process the information and send it to an AI model.

The AI would then generate a personalized daily fitness plan, including:

Workout Plan

  • Exercises for the day

  • Sets and repetitions

  • Workout duration

  • Rest periods

  • Gym/home workout variations

Daily Meal Plan

  • Breakfast

  • Lunch

  • Snacks

  • Dinner

  • Suggested food options

  • Approximate calorie and protein targets

Daily Targets

  • Estimated calorie target

  • Protein target

  • Water intake

  • Daily activity/step goal

  • Workout duration

Personalized Schedule
The system should ideally generate a plan based on the user’s goal and preferences and provide a different daily plan as the user progresses.

WhatsApp Automation

Once the plan is generated, I want n8n to automatically send it to the user through WhatsApp.

For example:

Good Morning, Rahul!

Goal: Weight Loss
Today’s Target: ~2,000 kcal
Water: 2.5–3 L

Today’s Workout
• Squats – 3 × 12
• Push-ups – 3 × 10
• Walking – 30 min

Breakfast
• Eggs + oats + fruit

Lunch
• Rice/roti + vegetables + protein source

Dinner
• …

Have a great workout!

I would also like to eventually add daily reminders, progress tracking, and possibly allow users to update their weight or progress through WhatsApp.

What I Need Help With

I would especially appreciate suggestions on:

  1. How should I structure the n8n workflow?

  2. Which nodes would be best for processing the Google Form/Google Sheets data?

  3. What is the best way to structure the AI prompt so that the generated plans are consistent and personalized?

  4. How should I maintain a user’s information and progress over multiple days?

  5. What is the best approach for sending the generated plan through WhatsApp?

  6. How can I create a system where the AI generates a new plan each day rather than repeating the same plan?

  7. What would be the best database/storage option for user profiles and progress?

  8. Are there any important things I should consider regarding fitness, nutrition, calorie calculations, and user safety?

I’m fairly new to building larger n8n workflows, so I would really appreciate a recommended architecture or example workflow that I can use as a starting point.

Thanks in advance!
I’d love to hear suggestions from anyone who has built similar AI + n8n + WhatsApp automation systems.

Hi Manish,
I’d recommend treating this as a stateful workflow rather than having the AI generate everything from scratch every day.

A solid architecture would be:

Google Forms → Google Sheets → n8n → Database → AI → WhatsApp

I’d keep the Google Sheet mainly as the intake layer and store the actual user profile, preferences, plan history, progress, and daily state in a database such as Supabase/Postgres.

For the n8n workflow, I’d split it into smaller workflows:

  1. User onboarding – validate the form data, create/update the user profile and generate the initial plan.

  2. Daily plan generation – a Cron/Schedule Trigger retrieves the user’s current profile + previous plans + latest progress, then sends structured data to the AI.

  3. WhatsApp delivery – send the generated plan through the WhatsApp API and log the delivery status.

  4. Progress updates – receive WhatsApp messages such as weight updates and store them in the database.

  5. Progress/reminder workflow – periodically check users who need reminders or plan adjustments.

For the AI, I would strongly recommend using structured JSON output rather than asking it to return formatted text directly. For example:

{
“daily_targets”: {},
“workout”: {},
“meals”: [],
“notes”: []
}

Then n8n can validate the response and format it into a WhatsApp message. This makes the workflow much more reliable and easier to maintain.

For daily variation, don’t simply tell the AI “create a different workout.” Pass the previous 7–14 days of plans, completed workouts, progress, and constraints into the prompt and explicitly define what should change while maintaining continuity.

I’d also keep calorie/protein calculations and other deterministic logic outside the LLM wherever possible. The AI should personalize and explain the plan, rather than being responsible for calculations that can be handled by code.

For WhatsApp, I’d use an official WhatsApp Business API provider and have n8n handle the orchestration, message formatting, scheduling, and logging.

One important consideration is safety: since this involves nutrition and fitness recommendations, I’d include validation rules for age, medical limitations, eating restrictions, extreme calorie targets, etc., and have the system avoid generating potentially unsafe recommendations.

If you’re new to larger n8n workflows, I’d definitely start with onboarding → database → daily generation → WhatsApp, and add progress tracking/reminders afterward. That will make debugging and scaling much easier.

I hope to collaborate with you in this project.
Best regards.

posts.name: Cindy Garcia
posts.cooked:
Hi Manish, I build n8n automations full time. Anatbil already gave you the right overall shape so I will not repeat it. Here are the four things that will actually bite you, roughly in the order they will bite.

1. There is no Google Forms trigger node in n8n. Most people find that out an hour in. Your two options are the Google Sheets trigger, which polls the responses sheet on a schedule, or an Apps Script onFormSubmit trigger on the form itself that posts to an n8n webhook. Use the second one. It fires the moment they hit submit, it hands you the answers as clean JSON instead of you mapping column letters, and it does not quietly break the first time someone inserts a column in that sheet. It is about fifteen lines of Apps Script and a UrlFetchApp call.

2. WhatsApp will not let you send the message in your example. This is the big one and it is worth knowing before you design around it. On the WhatsApp Business Cloud API you can only send a free form message inside 24 hours of the user’s last message to you. Your 7am plan is business initiated, so outside that window it has to be a pre approved template. And template variables cannot contain newlines, tabs, or more than four spaces in a row. So that nicely formatted plan with the bullets and the line breaks cannot go into a template parameter at all.

What does work: send a short approved utility template in the morning, something like “Good morning {{1}}, your plan for today is ready. Reply PLAN and I will send it.” Their reply opens the 24 hour window, and then you can send the full formatted plan as a normal message. You get a delivery signal and an engagement signal out of that for free, and it costs less. The other option is the template carries a link to a page with today’s plan on it. Either way, decide now rather than after your templates get rejected. Template messages are also billed per message at a rate that varies by country, so look up yours before you promise anyone a free daily service.

3. The daily fresh plan is the one part of the design I would change. Ask a model for a new day every morning and you do not get training, you get randomness. Progressive overload is the whole point of a program and it cannot exist if today has no idea what last Tuesday was. Generate a seven day block once a week instead, with the progression rules inside it, store the whole block as JSON, and let the daily job just render day N and send it. The daily job then needs no AI at all. Meals can come out of a bank you generated once per user and rotate, so nobody eats eggs and oats for ninety days straight. That is one AI call per user per week instead of seven, it is reproducible when a user tells you the plan looked wrong, and it is an actual program rather than a different workout every morning. The weekly regeneration is where you feed in the last block plus their check ins, which is the history point Anatbil was making.

4. Storage: three tables, not one sheet. Users for the profile, plans for one row per user per block with the JSON in it, checkins for weight and done or not done coming back off WhatsApp. Postgres or Supabase. Sheets will hold up until roughly your twentieth user, then the API quota and row locking start costing you plans that silently never sent.

Two operational things while you are in there. Store each user’s timezone and run the send job hourly, picking the users whose local time is now 7am, rather than one cron at 7am your time. And write a sent_at onto the plan row and select only rows where it is null, or the first time that job fails halfway through and you re run it, everyone who already got a message gets a second one.

On your safety question, which is the one I would push on hardest. I am a nurse, 30 years, 20 of them as a Director of Nursing at an outpatient surgery center, so I cannot let that one go by.

Calculate the calorie and protein numbers in code, Mifflin St Jeor plus an activity factor, and never let the model do the arithmetic. Then put a floor under it. A deficit past about 20 to 25 percent of maintenance is where people stop sleeping and quit, and no adult should be auto prescribed under roughly 1200 calories.

Compute BMI from their current weight and refuse the signup if the target weight puts them below 18.5. A weight loss bot that cheerfully helps an underweight nineteen year old lose eight more kilos is the thing that ends a project, and it will happen, because those are exactly the people who go looking for a free plan generator.

That “any conditions” free text box is a medical intake question whether you meant it as one or not. Pregnancy, insulin dependent diabetes, kidney disease, a heart condition, any history of an eating disorder: those need to route to a human or to a polite decline, not into the prompt as extra context. A standard high protein deficit plan is actively wrong in pregnancy and in reduced kidney function, and the model will not know to stop. Gate anyone under 18 out completely.

Then one plain disclaimer line in the very first message, and store the timestamp when they accept it.

None of that part needs AI. It is five if branches sitting in front of the model, and it is what makes the rest of this safe to send to a stranger.

Get the onboarding and the database piece running first, and if it breaks somewhere, post the workflow here and I will have a look at where.

Cindy Garcia, RN

Hey Manish, I’ve put together a few Form → AI → WhatsApp automations, so here’s the setup I’d recommend:

  • Collect: trigger on new Google Sheets rows, then a Code node works out calories and protein (Mifflin-St Jeor formula). Keep the numbers in code, use the AI only for writing the plan text.

  • Store: move profiles out of Sheets into Supabase or Postgres. Two tables are enough: one for users, one for daily logs (date, weight, what was sent).

  • Generate: a Schedule trigger every morning pulls active users. Give the AI the profile plus the last three plans and tell it not to repeat exercises. Ask for strict JSON (workout, meals, targets) and build the WhatsApp message from a template. This keeps plans consistent but fresh.

  • Send: go with the official WhatsApp Cloud API, unofficial gateways tend to get numbers banned. Keep in mind that scheduled morning messages outside the 24-hour window need an approved message template.

  • Track: a WhatsApp webhook catches replies like “weight 82”, saves them to the log and adjusts the targets.

  • Safety: set a minimum calorie limit, add a disclaimer, and have the flow decline plans for injuries or pregnancy.

Hi Manish,

I have extensively built and deployed production-grade, fault-tolerant AI orchestration pipelines matching this exact blueprint. Relying purely on basic AI loops for a stateful, daily progressing system like a fitness engine will cause runtime failures under real-world traffic.

Here is the bulletproof production architecture to solve your challenges:

  1. Data Ingestion & Schema Enforcement (Google Forms/Sheets to n8n)
    Do not pass raw webhook arrays directly to the LLM. You must place a custom JavaScript Code Node immediately after your Google Sheets Trigger. This node strips out payload defects, checks for missing data strings, and normalizes inputs into a strict, validated data frame before hitting the intelligence tier.

  2. Heavy Traffic & State Management (Redis Idempotency Layer)
    To prevent duplicate form submissions or duplicate webhook triggers from repeating identical workflows, deploy a tenant-scoped atomic idempotency lock using native Redis INCR or SETNX commands with a strict 24-hour TTL. If a duplicate trigger fires, the Redis Guard automatically throttles it within 1 millisecond, protecting your downstream LLM node from compute waste and double-costs.

  3. Structured AI Extraction (Frontier JSON Schemas)
    To ensure the AI generates consistent workout and meal plans every single day without hallucinating, configure advanced frontier models like Gemini or OpenAI using rigid responseSchemas directly at the API layer. This forces the model to strictly output data in a pre-defined JSON object, making it seamless for n8n to parse individual fields for WhatsApp.

  4. Daily Variation & Progress Tracking (Durable PostgreSQL Ledger)
    To prevent the AI from repeating the same fitness plan every day, you must decouple historical states. Split the pipeline into a durable relational database like PostgreSQL. For every daily submission or update, run a native Postgres Upsert Query (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET). This logs the user’s current weight, targets, and cumulative days. When generating today’s plan, feed the last 3 days of historical text from Postgres into the LLM context as a strict negative-prompt baseline (“Do not repeat these exercises/meals”).

  5. WhatsApp Delivery & Safety Guardrails
    Route the final validated payload asynchronously using a secure provider webhook like UltraMsg or Twilio. Never let the AI directly dictate critical metrics without deterministic checks. Set a rigid validation gate right before the WhatsApp node to evaluate calorie boundaries and flag extreme requests, ensuring 100% safety and absolute system uptime.

I have an active production engine built exactly on these deterministic principles (featuring Redis logic, custom JavaScript contracts, and Postgres upsert tables). I would be happy to share a visual canvas walkthrough or hop on a brief sync to help you deploy this successfully!

Hi @Manish_Kasan

Great project.

1. Workflow structure
Split it into 3 separate workflows instead of one big one:

  • Onboarding: form submitted → clean the data → calculate targets → save the profile → create the first plan → send it on WA
  • Daily plan: Schedule Trigger (e.g. 6 AM) → get active users → loop through each → pull their profile and recent history → AI → save → send
  • Incoming WA messages: a webhook that reads replies like “weight 72” or “done” → updates progress → sends a confirmation

Smaller workflows are much easier to debug and extend.

2. Nodes for the form data
Google Sheets Trigger (“row added”) works. Or skip Sheets and use the n8n Form node or Tally with a webhook, which is faster and cleaner. Then use Edit Fields (Set) to rename fields, a Code node for the maths, and Switch to branch by goal.

3. Consistent AI output
The biggest tip: Work out calories, protein and water in a Code node, then pass those numbers to the AI as fixed targets. Also:

  • Have the AI return JSON (a Structured Output Parser or JSON schema), not free text
  • Build the WA message from that JSON with a template in a Code node, so the format never changes
  • Put the rules in the system prompt (stay within the calorie target ±5%, only use allowed foods, and so on)

4 & 7. Storing user data and progress
Google Sheets is fine for testing. For real users, move to Supabase (Postgres) or Airtable. Use 3 tables:

  • users: profile, targets, phone number with country code, active yes/no
  • plans: user, date, plan JSON
  • progress: user, date, weight, workout done yes/no

5. Sending on WA
Use the official WA Cloud API (n8n has a node for it) or a provider like Twilio, Interakt, WATI or Gupshup. Two things to know:

  • Morning messages the user didn’t trigger need pre-approved template messages, because free-form messages only work within 24 hours of the user’s last message
  • Avoid unofficial WA libraries, because numbers get banned

6. A new plan each day
Send the AI the last 5–7 days of plans and tell it not to repeat meals or workouts. Better still, decide the day’s focus in code (Mon upper body, Tue lower body, Wed cardio…) and let the AI fill in the details. Every week or two, adjust calories based on weight change.

8. Safety (important)

  • Use the Mifflin-St Jeor formula plus an activity multiplier for calories
  • Set limits in code: a deficit of no more than about 500 kcal a day, and never go below a safe minimum
  • Protein: roughly 1.6–2 g per kg for muscle gain, a bit lower for general fitness
  • If someone lists a medical condition, injury or pregnancy, or is under 18, don’t let the AI create a plan. Flag it and suggest they see a professional
  • Add a short disclaimer, get their consent before messaging, and include a “STOP” keyword to unsubscribe
  • Treat health data carefully, because privacy laws (like India’s DPDP Act) apply

Store a training template per goal (e.g. 3-day full body for beginners, 4-day upper/lower for muscle gain) with a week counter and progression rules (add reps, then add weight, deload every 4th week). Idempotency: one row per user per day, checked before sending, so a re-run never sends twice.

Hi Manish,

Your flow is a good starting point. Here’s how I’d structure it, answering your questions in order.

  1. Workflow structure
    I’d split it into three small workflows instead of one big one:
  • Onboarding: a new form submission creates the user profile and calculates their targets.
  • Daily plan: a Schedule trigger runs each morning, loops over active users, generates today’s plan and sends it.
  • Inbound messages: a WhatsApp webhook lets users report weight or progress and updates their record.
    Keeping them separate makes each one easy to test and fix.

  1. Nodes for the form data
    Google Sheets Trigger (row added) works with your Google Form. Alternatively, n8n’s own Form Trigger can replace Google Forms entirely and gives you cleaner data. Then use Edit Fields (Set) to clean the values, and a Code node to validate them (age range, weight values, required fields) before anything goes to the AI.

  2. Prompt structure

  • Put the fixed rules in a system prompt and the user data in the user message.
  • Ask for strict JSON output (workout, meals, targets) and validate it in a Code node. Use a structured output parser, and retry once if the format is wrong.
  • Do the maths in code, not in the AI. Calculate BMR/TDEE (for example Mifflin-St Jeor), then set calories and protein by goal. The AI chooses the exercises and foods to hit those numbers, so the numbers stay consistent.

4 and 7. Storing user data and progress
Use a real database instead of Sheets once you have more than a few users: Postgres or Supabase is ideal, with tables for users, daily_plans, and progress_logs (weight, workouts done, date). Airtable also works for a prototype.

  1. WhatsApp
    Use the WhatsApp Business Cloud API (Meta), which n8n supports with its WhatsApp Business Cloud node, or Twilio. Note that business-initiated messages outside the 24-hour window must use pre-approved message templates, so plan for that early. The daily ‘Good morning’ message will normally be a template, and replies from the user open a 24-hour window for free-form messages.

  2. A new plan every day
    Send the AI the user’s last 5–7 days of plans and progress from the database, and tell it not to repeat the same exercises and meals and to progress the difficulty gradually. A weekly ‘phase’ (for example, volume week, strength week) also adds variety. Save each plan so the next run can see it.

  3. Safety and nutrition

  • Add a disclaimer and a short health screening in the form. For anyone with medical conditions, pregnancy or injuries, don’t give a plan. Suggest seeing a doctor instead.
  • Set hard limits in code: a minimum calorie floor, a maximum weekly weight-change rate, and no plans for users under 18 without extra handling.
  • Avoid medical claims, and treat the content as general guidance.
  • Health data is sensitive, so get consent, store it securely and let users delete it.
  • Log every plan and add an error branch that alerts you when the AI output fails validation.

If it would help, I’m happy to sketch the workflows or build a first version with you.

Hi Manish,

Building a personalized AI fitness and meal planner via n8n and WhatsApp Cloud API looks smooth in staging, but migrating this system to support active users creates critical infrastructure bottlenecks—specifically around user safety overrides, distributed state tracking, and duplicate webhook triggers.

If a user rapidly taps a button or resubmits forms while the LLM is computing a previous token stream, a naive n8n setup will choke, causing duplicate WhatsApp outgoing payloads or database row corruption.

Here is how to architecturally secure and structure your production workspace from first principles:

Preventing Concurrency Failures: To secure your analytical and progress ledgers (PostgreSQL/Supabase) against duplicate mutations under surge spikes, deploy native Redis lock primitives (INCR + TTL gates) as atomic idempotency boundaries directly within the data transit paths. This safely isolates state transitions across your webhook ingestion streams.
Rigid Validation Gates for User Safety: When dealing with biometric data, fitness limitations, or caloric calculations, do not pass raw Google Sheets string inputs blindly to an AI model. Wrap the extracted objects inside hardcoded Pydantic validation schemas. The prompt matrix must use strict JSON constraints, forcing the LLM to output predictable daily macros, rest periods, and alternate workout loops with a mandatory verification checkpoint before hitting WhatsApp.
Stateful Progress Tracking: Instead of fragile spreadsheets, offload user profiles and historical meal/workout logs into a relational database with strict indexing. Use n8n’s Code nodes to calculate baseline totals via medical-consensus formulas (like Harris-Benedict for BMR) before passing data to the LLM. This prevents hallucinated cost-drifts and guarantees consistent, progressive daily variations.
Failure Isolation: Route the WhatsApp Cloud API/Twilio request node’s error outputs within the same execution loop to a global Error Trigger system. This captures transport failures or 429 rate-limits instantly, sending alert traces to your staging console while keeping the primary worker active.

Hi Manish,
I’d recommend treating this as a stateful workflow rather than having the AI generate everything from scratch every day.

A solid architecture would be:

Google Forms → Google Sheets → n8n → Database → AI → WhatsApp

I’d keep the Google Sheet mainly as the intake layer and store the actual user profile, preferences, plan history, progress, and daily state in a database such as Supabase/Postgres.

{

“workout”: {},
“meals”: [],
“notes”: []
}

Then n8n can validate the response and format it into a WhatsApp message. This makes the workflow much more reliable and easier to maintain.

Hi Manish, I build n8n automations full time. Anatbil already gave you the right overall shape so I will not repeat it. Here are the four things that will actually bite you, roughly in the order they will bite.

1. There is no Google Forms trigger node in n8n. Most people find that out an hour in. Your two options are the Google Sheets trigger, which polls the responses sheet on a schedule, or an Apps Script onFormSubmit trigger on the form itself that posts to an n8n webhook. Use the second one. It fires the moment they hit submit, it hands you the answers as clean JSON instead of you mapping column letters, and it does not quietly break the first time someone inserts a column in that sheet. It is about fifteen lines of Apps Script and a UrlFetchApp call.

2. WhatsApp will not let you send the message in your example. This is the big one and it is worth knowing before you design around it. On the WhatsApp Business Cloud API you can only send a free form message inside 24 hours of the user’s last message to you. Your 7am plan is business initiated, so outside that window it has to be a pre approved template. And template variables cannot contain newlines, tabs, or more than four spaces in a row. So that nicely formatted plan with the bullets and the line breaks cannot go into a template parameter at all.

What does work: send a short approved utility template in the morning, something like “Good morning {{1}}, your plan for today is ready. Reply PLAN and I will send it.” Their reply opens the 24 hour window, and then you can send the full formatted plan as a normal message. You get a delivery signal and an engagement signal out of that for free, and it costs less. The other option is the template carries a link to a page with today’s plan on it. Either way, decide now rather than after your templates get rejected. Template messages are also billed per message at a rate that varies by country, so look up yours before you promise anyone a free daily service.

3. The daily fresh plan is the one part of the design I would change. Ask a model for a new day every morning and you do not get training, you get randomness. Progressive overload is the whole point of a program and it cannot exist if today has no idea what last Tuesday was. Generate a seven day block once a week instead, with the progression rules inside it, store the whole block as JSON, and let the daily job just render day N and send it. The daily job then needs no AI at all. Meals can come out of a bank you generated once per user and rotate, so nobody eats eggs and oats for ninety days straight. That is one AI call per user per week instead of seven, it is reproducible when a user tells you the plan looked wrong, and it is an actual program rather than a different workout every morning. The weekly regeneration is where you feed in the last block plus their check ins, which is the history point Anatbil was making.

4. Storage: three tables, not one sheet. Users for the profile, plans for one row per user per block with the JSON in it, checkins for weight and done or not done coming back off WhatsApp. Postgres or Supabase. Sheets will hold up until roughly your twentieth user, then the API quota and row locking start costing you plans that silently never sent.

Two operational things while you are in there. Store each user’s timezone and run the send job hourly, picking the users whose local time is now 7am, rather than one cron at 7am your time. And write a sent_at onto the plan row and select only rows where it is null, or the first time that job fails halfway through and you re run it, everyone who already got a message gets a second one.

On your safety question, which is the one I would push on hardest. I am a nurse, 30 years, 20 of them as a Director of Nursing at an outpatient surgery center, so I cannot let that one go by.

Calculate the calorie and protein numbers in code, Mifflin St Jeor plus an activity factor, and never let the model do the arithmetic. Then put a floor under it. A deficit past about 20 to 25 percent of maintenance is where people stop sleeping and quit, and no adult should be auto prescribed under roughly 1200 calories.

Compute BMI from their current weight and refuse the signup if the target weight puts them below 18.5. A weight loss bot that cheerfully helps an underweight nineteen year old lose eight more kilos is the thing that ends a project, and it will happen, because those are exactly the people who go looking for a free plan generator.

That “any conditions” free text box is a medical intake question whether you meant it as one or not. Pregnancy, insulin dependent diabetes, kidney disease, a heart condition, any history of an eating disorder: those need to route to a human or to a polite decline, not into the prompt as extra context. A standard high protein deficit plan is actively wrong in pregnancy and in reduced kidney function, and the model will not know to stop. Gate anyone under 18 out completely.

Then one plain disclaimer line in the very first message, and store the timestamp when they accept it.

None of that part needs AI. It is five if branches sitting in front of the model, and it is what makes the rest of this safe to send to a stranger.

Get the onboarding and the database piece running first, and if it breaks somewhere, post the workflow here and I will have a look at where.

I have extensively built and deployed production-grade, fault-tolerant AI orchestration pipelines matching this exact blueprint. Relying purely on basic AI loops for a stateful, daily progressing system like a fitness engine will cause runtime failures under real-world traffic.

Here is the bulletproof production architecture to solve your challenges:

  1. Data Ingestion & Schema Enforcement (Google Forms/Sheets to n8n)
    Do not pass raw webhook arrays directly to the LLM. You must place a custom JavaScript Code Node immediately after your Google Sheets Trigger. This node strips out payload defects, checks for missing data strings, and normalizes inputs into a strict, validated data frame before hitting the intelligence tier.

  2. Heavy Traffic & State Management (Redis Idempotency Layer)
    To prevent duplicate form submissions or duplicate webhook triggers from repeating identical workflows, deploy a tenant-scoped atomic idempotency lock using native Redis INCR or SETNX commands with a strict 24-hour TTL. If a duplicate trigger fires, the Redis Guard automatically throttles it within 1 millisecond, protecting your downstream LLM node from compute waste and double-costs.

  3. Structured AI Extraction (Frontier JSON Schemas)
    To ensure the AI generates consistent workout and meal plans every single day without hallucinating, configure advanced frontier models like Gemini or OpenAI using rigid responseSchemas directly at the API layer. This forces the model to strictly output data in a pre-defined JSON object, making it seamless for n8n to parse individual fields for WhatsApp.

  4. Daily Variation & Progress Tracking (Durable PostgreSQL Ledger)
    To prevent the AI from repeating the same fitness plan every day, you must decouple historical states. Split the pipeline into a durable relational database like PostgreSQL. For every daily submission or update, run a native Postgres Upsert Query (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET). This logs the user’s current weight, targets, and cumulative days. When generating today’s plan, feed the last 3 days of historical text from Postgres into the LLM context as a strict negative-prompt baseline (“Do not repeat these exercises/meals”).

  5. WhatsApp Delivery & Safety Guardrails
    Route the final validated payload asynchronously using a secure provider webhook like UltraMsg or Twilio. Never let the AI directly dictate critical metrics without deterministic checks. Set a rigid validation gate right before the WhatsApp node to evaluate calorie boundaries and flag extreme requests, ensuring 100% safety and absolute system uptime.

Hi everyone,

I’m currently working on an AI-powered fitness automation using n8n, and I would appreciate some guidance from the community on how to design the workflow properly.

The basic idea is to create an automated system where a user first fills out a Google Form with their personal fitness requirements. The form would collect information such as:

  • Dietary preferences

  • Food preferences/restrictions

  • Any relevant limitations or conditions they want the system to consider

Proposed n8n Workflow

I’m thinking of building something like:

Google Form → Google Sheets → n8n → AI → Personalized Fitness Plan → WhatsApp

After the user submits the form, n8n would collect and process the information and send it to an AI model.

The AI would then generate a personalized daily fitness plan, including:

Workout Plan

  • Exercises for the day

  • Sets and repetitions

  • Workout duration

  • Rest periods

  • Gym/home workout variations

Daily Meal Plan

  • Breakfast

  • Lunch

  • Snacks

  • Dinner

  • Suggested food options

  • Approximate calorie and protein targets

Hi @Manish_Kasan

Great project.

1. Workflow structure
Split it into 3 separate workflows instead of one big one:

  • Onboarding: form submitted → clean the data → calculate targets → save the profile → create the first plan → send it on WA
  • Daily plan: Schedule Trigger (e.g. 6 AM) → get active users → loop through each → pull their profile and recent history → AI → save → send
  • Incoming WA messages: a webhook that reads replies like “weight 72” or “done” → updates progress → sends a confirmation

Smaller workflows are much easier to debug and extend.

2. Nodes for the form data
Google Sheets Trigger (“row added”) works. Or skip Sheets and use the n8n Form node or Tally with a webhook, which is faster and cleaner. Then use Edit Fields (Set) to rename fields, a Code node for the maths, and Switch to branch by goal.

3. Consistent AI output
The biggest tip: Work out calories, protein and water in a Code node, then pass those numbers to the AI as fixed targets. Also:

  • Have the AI return JSON (a Structured Output Parser or JSON schema), not free text
  • Build the WA message from that JSON with a template in a Code node, so the format never changes
  • Put the rules in the system prompt (stay within the calorie target ±5%, only use allowed foods, and so on)

4 & 7. Storing user data and progress
Google Sheets is fine for testing. For real users, move to Supabase (Postgres) or Airtable. Use 3 tables:

  • users: profile, targets, phone number with country code, active yes/no
  • plans: user, date, plan JSON
  • progress: user, date, weight, workout done yes/no

5. Sending on WA
Use the official WA Cloud API (n8n has a node for it) or a provider like Twilio, Interakt, WATI or Gupshup. Two things to know:

  • Morning messages the user didn’t trigger need pre-approved template messages, because free-form messages only work within 24 hours of the user’s last message
  • Avoid unofficial WA libraries, because numbers get banned

6. A new plan each day
Send the AI the last 5–7 days of plans and tell it not to repeat meals or workouts. Better still, decide the day’s focus in code (Mon upper body, Tue lower body, Wed cardio…) and let the AI fill in the details. Every week or two, adjust calories based on weight change.

8. Safety (important)

  • Use the Mifflin-St Jeor formula plus an activity multiplier for calories
  • Set limits in code: a deficit of no more than about 500 kcal a day, and never go below a safe minimum
  • Protein: roughly 1.6–2 g per kg for muscle gain, a bit lower for general fitness
  • If someone lists a medical condition, injury or pregnancy, or is under 18, don’t let the AI create a plan. Flag it and suggest they see a professional
  • Add a short disclaimer, get their consent before messaging, and include a “STOP” keyword to unsubscribe
  • Treat health data carefully, because privacy laws (like India’s DPDP Act) apply

Hi Manish,

Your flow is a good starting point. Here’s how I’d structure it, answering your questions in order.

  1. Workflow structure
    I’d split it into three small workflows instead of one big one:
  • Onboarding: a new form submission creates the user profile and calculates their targets.
  • Daily plan: a Schedule trigger runs each morning, loops over active users, generates today’s plan and sends it.
  • Inbound messages: a WhatsApp webhook lets users report weight or progress and updates their record.
    Keeping them separate makes each one easy to test and fix.

  1. Nodes for the form data
    Google Sheets Trigger (row added) works with your Google Form. Alternatively, n8n’s own Form Trigger can replace Google Forms entirely and gives you cleaner data. Then use Edit Fields (Set) to clean the values, and a Code node to validate them (age range, weight values, required fields) before anything goes to the AI.

  2. Prompt structure

  • Put the fixed rules in a system prompt and the user data in the user message.
  • Ask for strict JSON output (workout, meals, targets) and validate it in a Code node. Use a structured output parser, and retry once if the format is wrong.
  • Do the maths in code, not in the AI. Calculate BMR/TDEE (for example Mifflin-St Jeor), then set calories and protein by goal. The AI chooses the exercises and foods to hit those numbers, so the numbers stay consistent.

4 and 7. Storing user data and progress
Use a real database instead of Sheets once you have more than a few users: Postgres or Supabase is ideal, with tables for users, daily_plans, and progress_logs (weight, workouts done, date). Airtable also works for a prototype.

  1. WhatsApp
    Use the WhatsApp Business Cloud API (Meta), which n8n supports with its WhatsApp Business Cloud node, or Twilio. Note that business-initiated messages outside the 24-hour window must use pre-approved message templates, so plan for that early. The daily ‘Good morning’ message will normally be a template, and replies from the user open a 24-hour window for free-form messages.

  2. A new plan every day
    Send the AI the user’s last 5–7 days of plans and progress from the database, and tell it not to repeat the same exercises and meals and to progress the difficulty gradually. A weekly ‘phase’ (for example, volume week, strength week) also adds variety. Save each plan so the next run can see it.

  3. Safety and nutrition

  • Add a disclaimer and a short health screening in the form. For anyone with medical conditions, pregnancy or injuries, don’t give a plan. Suggest seeing a doctor instead.
  • Set hard limits in code: a minimum calorie floor, a maximum weekly weight-change rate, and no plans for users under 18 without extra handling.
  • Avoid medical claims, and treat the content as general guidance.
  • Health data is sensitive, so get consent, store it securely and let users delete it.
  • Log every plan and add an error branch that alerts you when the AI output fails validation.

comments.text:
Hi Manish, I build n8n automations full time. Anatbil already gave you the right overall shape so I will not repeat it. Here are the four things that will actually bite you, roughly in the order they will bite. 
  1. There is no Google Forms trigger node in n8n.  Most people find that out an hour in. Your two options are the Google Sheets trigger, which polls the responses sheet on a schedule, or an Apps Script onFormSubmit trigger on the form itself that posts to an n8n webhook. Use the second one. It fires the moment they hit submit, it hands you the answers as clean JSON instead of you mapping column letters, and it does not quietly break the first time someone inserts a column in that sheet. It is about fifteen lines of Apps Script and a UrlFetchApp call. 
  2. WhatsApp will not let you send the message in your example.  This is the big one and it is worth knowing before you design around it. On the WhatsApp Business Cloud API you can only send a free form message inside 24 hours of the user’s last message to you. Your 7am plan is business initiated, so outside that window it has to be a pre approved template. And template variables cannot contain newlines, tabs, or more than four spaces in a row. So that nicely formatted plan with the bullets and the line breaks cannot go into a template parameter at all. 
 What does work: send a short approved utility template in the morning, something like “Good morning {{1}}, your plan for today is ready. Reply PLAN and I will send it.” Their reply opens the 24 hour window, and then you can send the full formatted plan as a normal message. You get a delivery signal and an engagement signal out of that for free, and it costs less. The other option is the template carries a link to a page with today’s plan on it. Either way, decide now rather than after your templates get rejected. Template messages are also billed per message at a rate that varies by country, so look up yours before you promise anyone a free daily service. 
  3. The daily fresh plan is the one part of the design I would change.  Ask a model for a new day every morning and you do not get training, you get randomness. Progressive overload is the whole point of a program and it cannot exist if today has no idea what last Tuesday was. Generate a seven day block once a week instead, with the progression rules inside it, store the whole block as JSON, and let the daily job just render day N and send it. The daily job then needs no AI at all. Meals can come out of a bank you generated once per user and rotate, so nobody eats eggs and oats for ninety days straight. That is one AI call per user per week instead of seven, it is reproducible when a user tells you the plan looked wrong, and it is an actual program rather than a different workout every morning. The weekly regeneration is where you feed in the last block plus their check ins, which is the history point Anatbil was making. 
  4. Storage: three tables, not one sheet.  Users for the profile, plans for one row per user per block with the JSON in it, checkins for weight and done or not done coming back off WhatsApp. Postgres or Supabase. Sheets will hold up until roughly your twentieth user, then the API quota and row locking start costing you plans that silently never sent. 
 Two operational things while you are in there. Store each user’s timezone and run the send job hourly, picking the users whose local time is now 7am, rather than one cron at 7am your time. And write a sent_at onto the plan row and select only rows where it is null, or the first time that job fails halfway through and you re run it, everyone who already got a message gets a second one. 
  On your safety question, which is the one I would push on hardest.  I am a nurse, 30 years, 20 of them as a Director of Nursing at an outpatient surgery center, so I cannot let that one go by. 
 Calculate the calorie and protein numbers in code, Mifflin St Jeor plus an activity factor, and never let the model do the arithmetic. Then put a floor under it. A deficit past about 20 to 25 percent of maintenance is where people stop sleeping and quit, and no adult should be auto prescribed under roughly 1200 calories. 
 Compute BMI from their current weight and refuse the signup if the target weight puts them below 18.5. A weight loss bot that cheerfully helps an underweight nineteen year old lose eight more kilos is the thing that ends a project, and it will happen, because those are exactly the people who go looking for a free plan generator. 
 That “any conditions” free text box is a medical intake question whether you meant it as one or not. Pregnancy, insulin dependent diabetes, kidney disease, a heart condition, any history of an eating disorder: those need to route to a human or to a polite decline, not into the prompt as extra context. A standard high protein deficit plan is actively wrong in pregnancy and in reduced kidney function, and the model will not know to stop. Gate anyone under 18 out completely. 
 Then one plain disclaimer line in the very first message, and store the timestamp when they accept it. 
 None of that part needs AI. It is five if branches sitting in front of the model, and it is what makes the rest of this safe to send to a stranger. 
 Get the onboarding and the database piece running first, and if it breaks somewhere, post the workflow here and I will have a look at where.

 Here is the bulletproof production architecture to solve your challenges: 
 
 
 Data Ingestion & Schema Enforcement (Google Forms/Sheets to n8n) 
Do not pass raw webhook arrays directly to the LLM. You must place a custom JavaScript Code Node immediately after your Google Sheets Trigger. To prevent duplicate form submissions or duplicate webhook triggers from repeating identical workflows, deploy a tenant-scoped atomic idempotency lock using native Redis INCR or SETNX commands with a strict 24-hour TTL. If a duplicate trigger fires, the Redis Guard automatically throttles it within 1 millisecond, protecting your downstream LLM node from compute waste and double-costs.

To ensure the AI generates consistent workout and meal plans every single day without hallucinating, configure advanced frontier models like Gemini or OpenAI using rigid responseSchemas directly at the API layer. This forces the model to strictly output data in a pre-defined JSON object, making it seamless for n8n to parse individual fields for WhatsApp.

To prevent the AI from repeating the same fitness plan every day, you must decouple historical states. Split the pipeline into a durable relational database like PostgreSQL.   Google Form → Google Sheets → n8n → AI → Personalized Fitness Plan → WhatsApp  
 After the user submits the form, n8n would collect and process the information and send it to an AI model. 
 The AI would then generate a  personalized daily fitness plan , including: 
    Workout Plan  
 
 
 Exercises for the day 
 
 
 Sets and repetitions 
 
 
 Workout duration 
 
 
 Rest periods 
 
 
 Gym/home workout variations 
 
 
    Daily Meal Plan  
 
 
 Breakfast 
 
 
 Lunch 
 
 
 Snacks 
 
 
 Dinner 
 
 
 Suggested food options 
 
 
 Approximate calorie and protein targets 
 
 
 
 
 Hi  @Manish_Kasan  
 Great project. 
 1. Workflow structure 
Split it into 3 separate workflows instead of one big one: 
 
 Onboarding: form submitted → clean the data → calculate targets → save the profile → create the first plan → send it on WA 
 Daily plan: Schedule Trigger (e.g. 6 AM) → get active users → loop through each → pull their profile and recent history → AI → save → send 
 Incoming WA messages: a webhook that reads replies like “weight 72” or “done” → updates progress → sends a confirmation 
 
 Smaller workflows are much easier to debug and extend. 
 2. Nodes for the form data 
Google Sheets Trigger (“row added”) works. Or skip Sheets and use the n8n Form node or Tally with a webhook, which is faster and cleaner. Then use Edit Fields (Set) to rename fields, a Code node for the maths, and Switch to branch by goal. 
 3. Consistent AI output 
The biggest tip: Work out calories, protein and water in a Code node, then pass those numbers to the AI as fixed targets. Also: 
 
 Have the AI return JSON (a Structured Output Parser or JSON schema), not free text 
 Build the WA message from that JSON with a template in a Code node, so the format never changes 
 Put the rules in the system prompt (stay within the calorie target ±5%, only use allowed foods, and so on) 
 
 4 & 7. Storing user data and progress 
Google Sheets is fine for testing. For real users, move to Supabase (Postgres) or Airtable. Use 3 tables: 
 
  users : profile, targets, phone number with country code, active yes/no 
  plans : user, date, plan JSON 
  progress : user, date, weight, workout done yes/no 
 
 5. Sending on WA 
Use the official WA Cloud API (n8n has a node for it) or a provider like Twilio, Interakt, WATI or Gupshup. Two things to know: 
 
 Morning messages the user didn’t trigger need pre-approved template messages, because free-form messages only work within 24 hours of the user’s last message 
 Avoid unofficial WA libraries, because numbers get banned 
 
 6. A new plan each day 
Send the AI the last 5–7 days of plans and tell it not to repeat meals or workouts. Better still, decide the day’s focus in code (Mon upper body, Tue lower body, Wed cardio…) and let the AI fill in the details. Every week or two, adjust calories based on weight change. 
 8. Safety (important) 
 
 Use the Mifflin-St Jeor formula plus an activity multiplier for calories 
 Set limits in code: a deficit of no more than about 500 kcal a day, and never go below a safe minimum 
 Protein: roughly 1.6–2 g per kg for muscle gain, a bit lower for general fitness 
 If someone lists a medical condition, injury or pregnancy, or is under 18, don’t let the AI create a plan. Flag it and suggest they see a professional 
 Add a short disclaimer, get their consent before messaging, and include a “STOP” keyword to unsubscribe 
 Treat health data carefully, because privacy laws (like India’s DPDP Act) apply
